title: Trump can’t stop insulting Ken Paxton. Why? | CNN Politics
text:
Source: CNN

Republicans’ hopes of holding their Senate majority might hinge on Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton more than anyone else.

And President Donald Trump seemingly can’t stop insulting him.

Trump has repeatedly made the case for Paxton — whom he endorsed over the safer candidate, incumbent GOP Sen. John Cornyn — in recent days. And over and over, he’s thickly layered it in insults directed at the way Paxton looks, dresses and speaks. Trump then assures any listeners that Paxton, despite how he presents, is actually a fantastic attorney general.

It’s both bizarre and entertaining, in a vintage Trump way — before American politics seemed to get heavier under the weight of controversial wars, more severe partisanship and increasing political violence.

But it all begs the question: What on earth is Trump doing? Does he really think this helps his candidate? Is there any strategy behind it?

It all started on September 2, when Trump alluded to Paxton being a bit of a slob no fewer than three separate times:

Trump continued ragging on Paxton on successive nights of the Republican midterm convention in Dallas this week.

On Wednesday, the president made it clear — in case there was any doubt — that he personally didn’t have much regard for how Paxton presents.

“Some may not like the way he dresses,” Trump said before slipping in a laugh line: “I don’t.”

He added later: “He may not dress right, he may not talk exactly perfectly, and he may not be the best-looking guy I’ve ever seen. But you know what he is? He’s the greatest attorney general in America.”

Trump then recounted the whole thing again on Thursday night, as the camera rather awkwardly cut to Paxton standing and bearing his latest indignity.

“So I don’t know if he’s gonna ever speak to me again, but you know, I don’t care as long as he wins,” Trump said. “I really don’t care.”

There are a few potential explanations for all this.

Occam’s razor could certainly apply here. Trump has made it abundantly clear throughout his time in the public eye that he really values personal appearance. He tends to select aides and Cabinet members who are TV-friendly and/or look the part.

Paxton certainly is not that. Look no further than thebrief videothat his campaign for some reason posted shortly before Trump started publicly ragging on him. Whatever Paxton’s assets, he most certainly lacks charisma.

It seems entirely possible, and potentially the simplest explanation, that Trump can’t get past how poorly Paxton presents, and he just doesn’t have a filter on the subject. He has preempted some of his criticism by claiming that his staff told him not to say it. Plus, it’s no secret that Trump-the-showman feeds off the energy of crowds, so maybe the reactions to his criticism are too hard for him to resist.

But assuming he has an actual strategy here, there are reasons it could make some sense.

One is that Trump is trying to focus on Paxton’s, well,less-offensiveliabilities.

This is a candidate with a host ofpersonal and professional scandals and problemsin his past. To the extent Trump gestures at how Paxton looks — rather than past criminal charges, an impeachment and infidelity allegations — and gets people to unconsciously think it’s just the way he presents himself that’s his big liability, maybe it’s a net-positive?

Trump could also be trying to draw attention to Paxton’s supposed competence. Part of the coverage of these comments, after all, includes Trump calling him a great and even unparalleled attorney general. Many media outlets likely wouldn’t cover those comments made on their own, but Trump suggesting Paxton is a slob means the quotes get more eyeballs.

Maybe by saying this over and over again, Trump is trying to focus voters on what should really matter in such a campaign.

But a final potential motivation is something more insidious. Perhaps Trump is setting the stage to blame Paxton for a potential loss.

Trump is a proud man, of course. He’s alreadypre-blaming congressional Republicansfor potentially losing the House and Senate (even though polling overwhelmingly suggests the party’s biggest problems are largely his doing).

If Paxton loses, it would be the first time the GOP lost a statewide race in Texas in more than 30 years. And given the central role Trump played in elevating Paxton, it would be a huge black mark on the president’s political record. After all, he was the one who helped Paxton defeat a much more standard-issue, scandal-free candidate in Cornyn, who likely would have had an easier time in the general election.

But perhaps Trump is creating some distance so he can later say Paxton ran a terrible campaign and didn’t take advantage of his opportunity. The president is clearly sensitive about failed endorsements and often tries to explain them away after the fact byblaming the candidate.

Thus far, the jury is out on how Trump’s antics are playing.

Trump claimed Wednesday that Paxton’s numbers were going “through the roof” since the president began ragging on him. But there’s no actual evidence of that. The polls generally show a margin-of-error race, and some show Democratic state Rep. James Talarico slightly ahead.

What’s pretty clear from those polls, though, is that Paxton hasn’t really rallied Republicans to his side after a brutal primary four months ago. So maybe Trump decided it’s worth trying something — anything — to give him a little boost.

He’s just chosen a very curious method.
